packet.headline_seed: On its 40th anniversary, we reassess 1986's SpaceCamp
packet.description_seed: Forty years ago, the future seemed just around the corner—and the vehicle that was going to take us there was NASA's Space Shuttle. Originally envisioned as part of a larger integrated space transportation system , the shuttle was billed as a fully reusable vehicle, totally unlike the one-and-done capsules of the fading Apollo era, capable of making monthly (and perhaps even weekly) ferry flights to low Earth orbit. The shuttle, it was hoped, would transform human space flight from extraordinary to mundane. Brands like Coke and Pepsi were quick to hop aboard and expand the Cola Wars into space , and there were even plans to blast Sesame Street's Big Bird into orbit . The loss of Challenger in January 1986—carrying educator Christa McAuliffe, who would have been the first private citizen in space—put the kibosh on all of that. The shuttle, while fantastically advanced, would never be the vehicle to help humankind slip all of our surly bonds, so to speak. Even operating at its most frantic peak in 1985 just before Challenger's loss, the shuttle hardware managed a maximum of nine flights in one calendar year; for most of the 1990s, it performed at five or six flights per year. Civilians in space—to say nothing of Big Bird—would have to wait. Read full article Comments

Originally envisioned as part of a larger integrated space transportation system, the shuttle was billed as a fully reusable vehicle, totally unlike the one-and-done capsules of the fading Apollo era, capable of making monthly (and perhaps even weekly) ferry flights to low Earth orbit. The shuttle, it was hoped, would transform human space flight from extraordinary to mundane. Brands like Coke and Pepsi were quick to hop aboard and expand the Cola Wars into space, and there were even plans to blast Sesame Street’s Big Bird into orbit.

The loss of Challenger in January 1986—carrying educator Christa McAuliffe, who would have been the first private citizen in space—put the kibosh on all of that. The shuttle, while fantastically advanced, would never be the vehicle to help humankind slip all of our surly bonds, so to speak. Even operating at its most frantic peak in 1985 just before Challenger’s loss, the shuttle hardware managed a maximum of nine flights in one calendar year; for most of the 1990s, it performed at five or six flights per year. Civilians in space—to say nothing of Big Bird—would have to wait.

For better or for worse, Fox chose to release the film, which ultimately made about $9.6 million on a reported $25 million budget. Ouch. Audiences, it seemed, weren’t really interested in watching a bunch of kids in peril on a space shuttle. Today, on the rare occasions SpaceCamp comes up in film discussions at all—usually among geeks of a certain age who encountered it when they were younger—it’s often spoken of with derision. Kids! Robots! Thermal curtain failures! Preposterous! But is it really a bad movie? It’s not currently available for streaming, but this is exactly the kind of scenario that physical media is made for. And so, with the movie’s 40th anniversary looming, Senior Space Editor Eric Berger and I grab

Forty years ago, the future seemed just around the corner—and the vehicle that was going to take us there was NASA’s Space Shuttle. Originally envisioned as part of a larger integrated space transportation system, the shuttle was billed as a fully reusable vehicle, totally unlike the one-and-done capsules of the fading Apollo era, capable of making monthly (and perhaps even weekly) ferry flights to low Earth orbit.

The shuttle, it was hoped, would transform human space flight from extraordinary to mundane. Brands like Coke and Pepsi were quick to hop aboard and expand the Cola Wars into space, and there were even plans to blast Sesame Street’s Big Bird into orbit.

The loss of Challenger in January 1986—carrying educator Christa McAuliffe, who would have been the first private citizen in space—put the kibosh on all of that. The shuttle, while fantastically advanced, would never be the vehicle to help humankind slip all of our surly bonds, so to speak. Even operating at its most frantic peak in 1985 just before Challenger’s loss, the shuttle hardware managed a maximum of nine flights in one calendar year; for most of the 1990s, it performed at five or six flights per year. Civilians in space—to say nothing of Big Bird—would have to wait.

And into that post-Challenger disillusioned summer of 1986, Hollywood brought us SpaceCamp. It had all the right ingredients: A stacked cast with a solid leading duo (Kate Capshaw and Tom Skerritt), tons of real NASA location footage, and a big, brassy score by none other than John Williams. The film was completed before the Challenger disaster, leaving 20th Century Fox with something of a nightmarish choice on their hands—to shelve the film and lose millions, or send it to theaters and risk a PR disaster.

For better or for worse, Fox chose to release the film, which ultimately made about $9.6 million on a reported $25 million budget. Ouch. Audiences, it seemed, weren’t really interested in watching a bunch of kids in peril on a space shuttle. Today, on the rare occasions SpaceCamp comes up in film discussions at all—usually among geeks of a certain age who encountered it when they were younger—it’s often spoken of with derision. Kids! payload.title: SpaceCamp-elokuvan 40-vuotishetki nostaa esiin sukkula-ajan lupaukset ja pettymykset
payload.summary: Vuoden 1986 SpaceCamp-elokuvaa tarkastellaan uudelleen sen 40-vuotisjuhlavuoden lähestyessä. Elokuva syntyi aikana, jolloin NASA:n avaruussukkulaa pidettiin arkipäiväistyvän avaruuslentämisen symbolina, mutta Challengerin onnettomuus muutti nopeasti sekä tunnelman että odotukset.
payload.content:
Vuonna 1986 julkaistu SpaceCamp palaa arvioitavaksi 40-vuotisjuhlavuotensa kynnyksellä, ja samalla huomio kohdistuu aikakauteen, jossa NASA:n avaruussukkulaan liitettiin suuria lupauksia. Sukkulan uskottiin muuttavan ihmisten avaruuslennot poikkeuksellisista saavutuksista säännöllisemmäksi liikenteeksi, mutta Challengerin tuho tammikuussa 1986 pysäytti tämän mielikuvan rajusti.

## Sukkula nähtiin uuden ajan kulkuneuvona

Avaruussukkula suunniteltiin osaksi laajempaa avaruusliikenteen järjestelmää, ja sitä markkinoitiin uudelleenkäytettävänä aluksena, joka poikkesi Apollo-kauden kertakäyttöisistä kapseleista. Odotuksissa oli, että sukkula voisi lentää matalalle Maan kiertoradalle kuukausittain ja ehkä jopa viikoittain.

Tämä optimismi näkyi myös populaarikulttuurissa ja kaupallisissa suunnitelmissa. Coca-Colan ja Pepsin kaltaiset brändit pyrkivät mukaan avaruuteen, ja jopa Sesame Street -sarjan Big Bird -hahmoa kaavailtiin kiertoradalle. Ajatus siviileistä avaruudessa ei ollut enää vain tieteiskuvitelmaa, vaan osa ajan julkista avaruuspuhetta.

## Challenger muutti SpaceCampin taustan

Challengerin onnettomuudessa tammikuussa 1986 kuoli muun miehistön mukana opettaja Christa McAuliffe, josta olisi tullut ensimmäinen yksityishenkilö avaruudessa. Tapaus muutti äkillisesti sen ilmapiirin, jossa SpaceCamp saapui yleisön eteen. Elokuva, jossa lapset joutuvat vaaraan avaruussukkulassa, julkaistiin tragedian jälkeen poikkeuksellisen vaikeassa tilanteessa.

Fox päätti silti tuoda elokuvan levitykseen. Se tuotti lopulta noin 9,6 miljoonaa dollaria, kun sen budjetiksi kerrotaan noin 25 miljoonaa dollaria. Yleisö ei vaikuttanut innostuneen tarinasta, jossa nuoret ovat hengenvaarassa sukkulassa.

## Maine jäi ristiriitaiseksi

SpaceCamp muistetaan nykyisin lähinnä satunnaisissa elokuvakeskusteluissa, usein pilkallisessa sävyssä. Sen aineksia ovat lapset, robotit ja tekniset uhkat, jotka voivat kuulostaa jälkikäteen kömpelöiltä. Uudelleenarvioinnin kiinnostavuus syntyy kuitenkin juuri tästä ristiriidasta: elokuva ei ole vain erillinen seikkailufilmi, vaan kuva hetkestä, jolloin avaruussukkulan lupaus törmäsi todellisuuden rajoihin.

Sukkula oli teknisesti vaikuttava järjestelmä, mutta siitä ei tullut niin tiheästi lentävää arkista avaruusbussia kuin 1980-luvun alun puheissa toivottiin. Vuonna 1985 lentoja oli enimmillään yhdeksän vuodessa, ja 1990-luvulla määrä jäi useimmiten viiteen tai kuuteen lentoon vuodessa. SpaceCampin perintö on siksi myös muistutus siitä, kuinka nopeasti teknologinen optimismi voi muuttua varovaisuudeksi.
summary_bullets: Elokuva julkaistiin Challengerin onnettomuuden jälkeen vaikeassa ilmapiirissä.
Avaruussukkulan alkuperäiset odotukset säännöllisestä avaruusliikenteestä eivät toteutuneet.
payload.journalist_note: Artikkeli perustuu yhteen lähdepakettiin ja käsittelee aihetta rajatusti: SpaceCampin uudelleenarviointia, sen julkaisukontekstia sekä avaruussukkulan 1980-luvun odotuksia. En lisännyt lähteen ulkopuolisia juoni- tai tuotantotietoja.

Forty years ago, the future seemed just around the corner—and the vehicle that was going to take us there was NASA’s Space Shuttle. Originally envisioned as part of a larger integrated space transportation system, the shuttle was billed as a fully reusable vehicle, totally unlike the one-and-done capsules of the fading Apollo era, capable of making monthly (and perhaps even weekly) ferry flights to low Earth orbit. The shuttle, it was hoped, would transform human space flight from extraordinary to mundane. Brands like Coke and Pepsi were quick to hop aboard and expand the Cola Wars into space, and there were even plans to blast Sesame Street’s Big Bird into orbit.

The loss of Challenger in January 1986—carrying educator Christa McAuliffe, who would have been the first private citizen in space—put the kibosh on all of that. The shuttle, while fantastically advanced, would never be the vehicle to help humankind slip all of our surly bonds, so to speak. Even operating at its most frantic peak in 1985 just before Challenger’s loss, the shuttle hardware managed a maximum of nine flights in one calendar year; for most of the 1990s, it performed at five or six flights per year. Civilians in space—to say nothing of Big Bird—would have to wait.

For better or for worse, Fox chose to release the film, which ultimately made about $9.6 million on a reported $25 million budget. Ouch. Audiences, it seemed, weren’t really interested in watching a bunch of kids in peril on a space shuttle. Today, on the rare occasions SpaceCamp comes up in film discussions at all—usually among geeks of a certain age who encountered it when they were younger—it’s often spoken of with derision. Kids! Robots! Thermal curtain failures! Preposterous! But is it really a bad movie? It’s not currently available for streaming, but this is exactly the kind of scenario that physical media is made for.
